# A Note on AI Assistance {.unnumbered}

::: {.callout-note title="Working draft"}
**This text is an evolving working draft.** As I collect ideas and organize this material, these chapters represent an active work in progress. While I develop each section carefully from foundational literature and verified computation cells, I have not yet reached the stage of stress-testing these frameworks with external domain experts. I am sharing this draft openly to organize my thoughts and invite early community feedback as the curriculum takes shape.
:::

This book is released as an open-access, living textbook; it is not yet under contract with a commercial publisher. Unlike established engineering disciplines with decades of pedagogical consensus, the field of agentic systems is nascent, explosive, and exceptionally fluid. Because systems architectures for autonomous machine learning are moving week by week, I am sharing these chapters as an open research notebook rather than holding them back for a multi-year publishing cycle.

Every textbook begins with collecting ideas, organizing scattered concepts, and structuring outlines: deciding what needs to be a chapter, what belongs in a section, and crucially, what not to cover. In developing this text, I used artificial intelligence to help explore how to structure the pieces together, discover relevant literature, and organize the resulting curriculum.

In this book, I frame the discipline through the conceptual lens of the *stochastic computer*—examining how to engineer reliable, deterministic software runtimes around inherently non-deterministic, probabilistic foundation models. To explore this architecture, I used an agentic approach to write about agentic systems. I collaborated with multi-agent workflows to brainstorm taxonomies, explore alternative structural framings, and debate architectural trade-offs. To test pedagogical clarity, I prompted agent personas with diverse student backgrounds to probe where my explanations broke down, reveal conceptual blind spots, and help me work backward to clarify the exposition. I pushed the methodology further by orchestrating simulated panels of domain specialists—systems architects, runtime developers, and benchmark evaluators—to critique draft chapters from multiple perspectives before human review.

Yet simulated feedback and AI-assisted drafting can never replace human engineering. An early attempt to orchestrate an unconstrained multi-step agentic pipeline to write sections of this book failed decisively, demonstrating firsthand why autonomous agents cannot replace human synthesis. Setting up context boundaries, execution sandboxes, and alignment guardrails to help models collaborate constructively provided immediate, practical insight into the exact systems challenges this book analyzes.

A textbook is fundamentally a distillation; the primary credit belongs to the researchers whose papers made the foundational discoveries and whose work populates our bibliography. At the same time, tools do not write textbooks. Assembling those discoveries into a coherent, teachable systems narrative requires demanding labor, late nights, and iterative rewriting: defining the abstractions, constructing executable models, and refining the text. Authorship is the assumption of that responsibility—to curate the material with integrity and to serve as the human point of contact when a reader finds an error or an engineer offers a critique.

Because this field is moving rapidly and the curriculum is actively taking shape, this text represents an evolving working draft. While the embedded code cells execute and the automated test suite checks reference hygiene, I am still in the process of organizing my thoughts and developing the material before taking it through the extensive expert stress-testing that will precede final publication. I encourage readers, practitioners, and researchers to read thoughtfully, report flaws on GitHub, and help shape this draft as it matures.

The principle holds with special force when the subject itself is autonomous: **the tool can propose, and the tool can simulate, but only the human engineer can ratify and take responsibility.**
